description: We are a group of folks super interested in GeoAI, the crossover between geospatial data, satellite imagery, and artificial intelligence. We like taking complex location data and real-world earth/space observation data and turning it into something genuinely useful.
summary: Farmers choose next year's crops in autumn, months before they know whether summer will bring the heat that halved Prairie yields in 2021. Field Shift is a free rotation planner with a Canada side and a US side. In Saskatchewan it links NASA POWER weather, MODIS greenness and SoilGrids soil water to 40+ years of real yields for 10 districts and 8 crops, and replays 44 past summers against every rotation the agronomic rules allow. On the US side it starts from a corn–soybean farm's water, equipment and market limits and backs three ways to diversify with a long-term Iowa field trial and on-farm trials, set on a county map of the United States. On both sides we tested whether next season can be forecast or rotations ranked, and neither holds up. So the planner does neither. It shows which options a farm can actually grow, which held up about the same, what really differs between them (the drought year and the dollars), and what is still unknown, then hands a one-page summary to the local agronomist. In season, the Saskatchewan model explains about 59% of year-to-year yield swings.
details:
WHAT IT DOES. One demo, two sides. A switch at the top of every page moves between Canada and the US.

Canada side (Saskatchewan), a four-step planner: your field, what matters, explore options, review together. The farmer picks a district on the map, the crops grown in 2026 and 2025, their usual plan, and the crops they can't grow or haven't checked. The planner returns how many rotations held up about the same on average and whether the usual plan is one of them; a chart of every allowed rotation by what it kept in a 2021-like drought and $/ac at 2026 guide prices, the two things that really differ; three option cards (usual plan, best in 2021, highest $/ac), labelled by what they are good at, not ranked; in-season alerts with how often each fired since 1982; and a one-page summary for the agronomist. Example, Sherwood district, after wheat: 15 rotations held up about the same (100–103% of a normal crop), the usual canola → wheat among them. In 2021, lentil → wheat kept about 80% of a normal crop against about 43% for canola → wheat. At 2026 prices, lentil → canola earns about $227/ac a year against $133.

US side, a research explorer on one page. Map: every US county, with the seven study sites, how closely each county's climate resembles them, and where each number comes from. Farm priorities: a corn–soybean farmer in Iowa enters water source, equipment, an oat buyer and priorities, and compares corn–soybeans, corn–soybeans with winter rye, and a three-year rotation with oats and red clover; an option the farm cannot do is flagged, and anything not checked stays an open question. Trial evidence: year-by-year results from the Marsden long-term rotation trial and five on-farm rye trials, negative and non-significant outcomes included. Model check: how far the process model is from field records, for every assumption tried. Sources: evidence panels with links and downloads.

HOW IT WORKS.

1. Screen. Rotation rules (canola and lentil 2-year break, flax 3 years, no pulse after pulse) and farm limits remove what can't be grown. Unknown answers are kept as questions, never scored as zero.

2. Replay. Past summers are replayed as possible futures. Each crop is scored against its own normal yield, so no price guess is needed. In Saskatchewan a gradient-boosting model on NASA POWER season features, SoilGrids soil water and in-season MODIS NDVI drives the replay, tested by hiding one whole year at a time.

3. Ground. Rotation effects are measured, not assumed: yield by previous crop on Manitoba fields (MASC) for Canada, and the Marsden long-term trial for Iowa (96 paired comparisons; in locked test years 2012–2017 the three-year system yielded +10.2 bu/ac corn and +6.2 bu/ac soybeans over the two-year system).

4. Gate. Every claim carries its scale (field, district, region) and whether it passed a test fixed before running. What failed is reported too.

RESULTS, TESTED HONESTLY.

- No forecast is possible before planting, on either side. In Saskatchewan pre-season models do no better than "assume a normal year", El Niño included. In the US, a process model beat the county's own past mean in only 2 of 9 county × crop series.

- Once the season is under way (Saskatchewan): average error 18.8% of a normal crop against 22.2% for trend only; about 59% of year-to-year swings explained; 55% of bad years flagged with 13% false alarms. The clearest driver is more than 15 days above 30 °C at flowering, which cuts yield by about 20%.

- Twenty ideas, one written rule. Selection on 1982–2017, then a one-time exam on untouched 2018–2025. Only two passed both, and both are new data: MODIS NDVI and SoilGrids soil water.

- Backtest, picks made from past data only, 6 districts never used for tuning: in the 2021 drought the advice kept 61% of a normal crop against 50% for canola → wheat. Its single worst year was lower (39% against 50%), and we say so.

- Rotations can't be honestly ranked. In Saskatchewan 5–15 rotations per district are tied within 2 points. In Iowa the published economic order flips with the technology package.

- Where the approach stops. The fitted in-season Saskatchewan model transfers to rain-fed Kansas (about 62% of swings for corn, sorghum and soybeans). It does not transfer to irrigated, forage-heavy Idaho counties, and the Iowa process model has not passed field validation (corn bias −15.0 to −9.5 bu/ac in the 2014 replay), so the US side shows no yield or profit prediction.

- Independent re-check: a re-run from a clean copy reproduced every Saskatchewan headline number and found no data leakage.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT. A farmer gets a local, plain view of how their options held up when summers went wrong, and a short list of what to settle with their agronomist. It is free, works on a phone and sends nothing anywhere. The tool supports the agronomist and doesn't replace them.

CREATIVITY. The planner replays the past where a forecast can't be made, labels options by what they are good at where a ranking isn't reliable, and treats "not checked" as a question, not a penalty. Two methods, one statistical and one built on field trials, were held to the same standard and reached the same boundary.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED. District and county averages are not fields; regional NASA weather is not field-measured soil water. A rotation is a multi-year decision bound by agronomic rules, equipment, water and markets. Prices swing, so yield decides and $/ac is shown beside it. Small data: about 44 summers and about 5 droughts per place. Satellite pixel purity: 3 of 10 Saskatchewan NDVI boxes cover towns, which we checked and documented. Third-party trial data and papers keep their own licences.

TOOLS. Python (pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, SHAP, matplotlib), Rust (independent reduced water–carbon–nitrogen model), plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript for the demo, GitHub
